manuscript_title: Patch-Clamp Single-Cell Proteomics in Acute Brain Slices: A Framework for Recording, Retrieval, and Interpretation

required_revisions.text: Requalify the capacitance–protein-identification correlation (Fig 3D). Report the raw capacitance and protein-ID values for all three gigaseal-preserved neurons, and the in-situ-to-during-retrieval capacitance delta for each (a direct test of whether retrieval damage, not soma size, drives the correlation). Remove the adjusted R²=0.998 framing (a mathematical artefact of fitting a line to three points with 1 df); report a bootstrapped confidence interval or explicitly state the finding as a feasibility demonstration on three observations, not a validated association. Scale every related sentence (abstract, Results, Conclusions) to 'three observations'.

Reframe the spike-integrity/synaptic-protein-enrichment association (Fig 4) as a hypothesis-generating observation, not a demonstrated association. It rests on one neuron per condition (#4 stable, #7 reduced amplitude, #6 single spike) and is partly confounded by construction (spike integrity and synaptic protein recovery are both consequences of the same retrieval damage). Either present it as qualitative observation with explicit n=1 caveats or remove the comparative language.

Reframe the 'decoupling' claim (Fig 5C–D) as a preliminary null result. With n=6 the power to detect a correlation is minimal; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and the pooled heterogeneous outcomes (no gigaseal, gigaseal lost, torn) could dilute a real size effect. State this limitation explicitly, or add an equivalence test if the claim is that the correlation is truly absent.
Provide the derivation of the '25–50% of the soma could be lost' estimate from the capacitance changes in Fig 3C, or remove the claim. As written it has no stated basis.

Complete the reproducibility record: (a) resolve the placeholder Supporting Information DOI ('https://pubs.acs.org/doi/xxxxxxxxxxx/') and confirm Tables S1–S3 are accessible there; (b) give a versioned code repository (specific repo name, commit hash or tag, or a Zenodo DOI) rather than the bare user URL; (c) specify the SynGO database version/date, the enrichment algorithm, the background distribution, the minimum gene-set size, and the multiple-comparison correction behind the Q-values; (d) specify PCA preprocessing (normalization, imputation, scaling), number of components, and variance explained by PC1/PC2; (e) report exact p-values (e.g., for F=1577 with df=1,1) rather than 'p<0.05'; (f) justify or remove the log transformation of capacitance.

Add a statistics subsection and complete the methods reporting: state what error bars/ribbons represent (SD/SEM/CI) wherever they appear; name the statistical test for every comparison; state the sex of the animals, the number of animals used (12 neurons from how many rats?), genotype/background, and housing conditions; add a randomization/blinding statement; state whether the 12 neurons are biological or technical replicates; provide chemical vendors and catalog numbers (or CAS) for the internal solution, aCSF, DDM, and trypsin; state the UniProt release date, LC gradient profile (%B over time) and column temperature, and the FAIMS CV scheme (single vs multiple).

Fix the citation record: remove or replace Ref 31 (Guo et al., saxitoxin total synthesis), which is implausibly non-germane to the slice-electrophysiology methods claim it is cited for; complete the incomplete entries for Refs 30, 15, and 24 (volume/pages/DOI); remove the 'For Table of Contents Only' artifact entry (#34); confirm whether Refs 8 and 9 actually impose the 'all-or-nothing' protein-identification thresholds described, and cite the relevant methods sentence if so.

Address the competing preprint (Johnson et al. 2026, bioRxiv, doi:10.64898/2026.04.22.720006, 'aspiration patch proteomics') if it was available at the time of preparation, and state explicitly what whole-soma retrieval adds over the cytoplasmic-aspiration approaches of Choi 2022 and Lee 2024 beyond higher protein counts.

Benchmark the transmembrane-protein coverage (Fig 7, S4, S5): state the minimal detectable expression threshold and how the 4–27 ion-channel-subunit recovery compares to expected copy numbers of GABRA1, SCN2A, GRM3 etc. in a single mPFC L2/3 pyramidal soma, and report the PSM-level FDR / unique-peptide evidence for low-abundance targets (including SST and VGF, with sequence coverage and PSM counts).

minor_suggestions: Define 'shotgun patch-SCP' at first use in the abstract/introduction rather than leaving the reader to infer it from the Results.
State the torn-neuron protein counts explicitly so the reader can compare categories quantitatively (the text gives ranges for no-gigaseal retrievals but not for torn neurons).
For the PCA (Fig 6A), state whether the clustering is robust to normalization/scaling choices and whether it reflects retrieval quality rather than total protein yield driving the first component.

Report the variance explained by the first two principal components and whether clustering was tested against measured confounds (neuron depth in slice, time after slice preparation, cell size from DIC images).

State whether the per-neuron SynGO gene lists were normalized for the number of detected proteins, so the reader can assess whether the apparent lack of synaptic enrichment in neuron #6 reflects lower total IDs rather than selective loss.
Specify R package versions (ComplexHeatmap, ggplot2, UpSetR) and the compute environment, and add a random seed for any stochastic analysis.
Consider a head-to-head (even qualitative) comparison of the present whole-soma framework against what was already achievable with cytoplasmic aspiration in slices, to sharpen the novelty claim.
Consider prospectively defining an inclusion criterion for 'high-context retrieval' (e.g., capacitance threshold, spiking amplitude during relocation) to be tested on an independent set of neurons.

weaknesses.text: LOAD-BEARING WEAKNESS 1: Claim that 'gigaseal preservation provides a quantitative bridge between proteomics and electrophysiology' (abstract, Results) is based on n=3 neurons, with a linear regression (F=1577, p<0.05, adjusted R²=0.998) that has 1 degree of freedom. With three points, any two-species relationship (linear, log, or otherwise) is trivially overfitted, and the reported R² ≈ 1.0 is a mathematical artefact of fitting a line to two degrees of freedom, not evidence of a real correlation. The claim that capacitance 'correlated' with protein IDs is technically true in a narrow statistical sense but cannot bear the interpretive weight placed on it. The authors should state explicitly that this finding is a demonstration of feasibility with three observations, not a validated association.

LOAD-BEARING WEAKNESS 2: The central comparative claim — that preservation of spiking during retrieval 'tended to be associated with broader synaptic enrichment' — rests on a visual comparison of three individual neurons (Neurons #4, #6, #7). No statistical test is applied to compare the SynGO term enrichment across the three groups (gigaseal-preserved, gigaseal-lost, no gigaseal, torn). The heatmap in Figure 6B and the UpSet plot in Figure 4B are displayed as exploratory visualisations, but the text states this as a finding. The sample size (1–3 neurons per condition) precludes any claim about association, tendency, or trend. The authors should either (a) present this as qualitative observation with explicit caveats about sample size, or (b) remove the comparative language.

LOAD-BEARING WEAKNESS 3: The paper presents its 'shotgun' indiscriminate-collection strategy as a methodological innovation, but the key claim — that 'comprehensive analysis can distinguish between high- and low-context retrievals' (Results, PCA section) — is not established by the PCA plot (Figure 6A). The authors state that torn neurons 'clustered apart from all others', but with n=2 torn neurons and the PCA presumably performed on all protein IDs (not just informative features), this separation could reflect global loss of signal rather than meaningful biological categorisation. Moreover, the claim that 'variation in proteomic profiles across retrieval outcomes reflected differences in biological insight' (Discussion) is a circular argument if the same data (protein IDs) are used both to cluster and to interpret the clusters. The authors need to demonstrate that the clustering is driven by synaptic/functional proteins, not by trivial abundance differences.

SOFT: Abstract states that 'preservation of neuronal spiking during relocation tended to be associated with broader synaptic enrichment' — the word 'tended' is a hedge, but the evidence is a single neuron (#4) compared with one partially compromised neuron (#7) and one aspirated neuron (#6). This is a report of three individual observations, not a tendency, and should be labelled as such.

SOFT: The title claims 'A Framework for Recording, Retrieval, and Interpretation' — what is presented is a preliminary schema for thinking about retrieval, not a validated framework with demonstrated generalisability. The word 'Framework' overstates what a single dataset of 12 neurons can establish.

SOFT: The authors state that '1500 proteins were identified' across the gigaseal-preserved neurons, and that 'at least 1700 total proteins were detected in each.' These are presented as impressive numbers, but without any normalisation (e.g., to cell size, or to the known numbers from bulk tissue or FACS-sorted populations), the reader cannot assess whether this is deep or shallow coverage. A benchmark comparison to a published single-neuron dataset would help.

SOFT: In the Discussion, the authors claim that 'retrieval mechanics, rather than in situ electrophysiology alone, limit whether proteins...are recovered' — this is a plausible conclusion from the data but the phrasing implies it is an established finding. The evidence is entirely consistent with the alternative explanation that the torn/aspirated neurons were simply smaller to begin with (but Fig 5C–D shows no correlation with in situ capacitance, so the data actually disfavour that alternative — which the authors should state more explicitly as support for their claim, while still acknowledging the tiny n).

SOFT: The paper mentions that 'a peptide that maps to transient receptor potential channels' was observed but 'ambiguous assignments precluded its confident inclusion' — this is honest but raises the question of whether the same ambiguity affects other transmembrane-protein assignments. The authors should state the FDR at the PSM level for these low-abundance targets, or acknowledge that transmembrane-protein detection is at the ragged edge of the method's sensitivity.

questions: Neuron #4 is presented as the 'ideal retrieval.' Could you provide the quantitative passive-membrane values (C, RM, VM) recorded during retrieval for all three gigaseal-preserved neurons, rather than only the ladder-plot deltas?

The linear regression of protein IDs vs log-capacitance (Fig 3D) reports adjusted R² = 0.998 with n=3. What are the raw protein-ID counts and capacitance values for the three neurons, and would you report the regression without the adjusted-R² correction given the sample size?

For the SynGO enrichment analyses (Figs 4B–C, 6B), what threshold was used to define 'enriched' versus 'not enriched' — the Q < 0.05 cutoff, or was additional filtering applied? Were the per-neuron gene lists filtered by any minimum spectral-count or intensity threshold, or simply by detection at 1% FDR?

The PCA in Figure 6A: how many components were considered, what proportion of variance do PC1 and PC2 explain, and was the PCA performed on raw LFQ intensities or on binary (detected/not-detected) data?
You detect somatostatin (SST) and VGF neuropeptides. Were these identified by unique peptides, and what were the sequence coverage and number of PSMs per sample?

weaknesses.text: Correlation between capacitance and protein identifications (Figs 3D, 3E) is supported by a linear regression on n=3 points; with three data points any line fits almost perfectly, and the reported adjusted R² of 0.998 and p<0.05 are an artefact of the sample size. Three neurons may also differ in cell type, health, time from slice preparation, or operator skill, none of which is controlled.

Association between active property preservation and synaptic protein recovery (Figs 4A–4C) rests on a single example per retrieval outcome (neuron #4 stable spiking, neuron #7 reduced amplitude, neuron #6 single spike). With n=1 per category, any difference in SynGO enrichment could reflect cell-to-cell variability, slice health, or technical variation in MS coverage.

Retrieval outcomes (gigaseal preserved, lost, no gigaseal, torn) are not controlled—they arise from mechanical success or failure, not random assignment. Neurons easier to retrieve may differ systematically (size, adhesion, cell type, slice location). Proteomic differences between categories could reflect pre-existing biological differences rather than retrieval integrity.

The 'shotgun' indiscriminate-collection strategy is presented as a framework but no comparison is made to the alternative (e.g., pre-specified inclusion criteria). The utility of the framework is asserted but not tested.
Sample size (n=12 total, n=3 for the key gigaseal-preserved group) is too small for reliable statistical inference; no power analysis is provided.
No blinding or randomisation is described for electrophysiology recordings, soma retrieval, or MS analysis; subjective decisions (e.g., when to apply suction) could influence outcomes.
Per-neuron SynGO analyses use a single run per neuron; with n=1 per cell enrichment Q-values are unstable and should be interpreted as exploratory, not confirmatory.
Number of neurons attempted vs successfully retrieved is not reported, so selection bias cannot be assessed.
Correlation analysis in Figure 3 uses log-transformed capacitance without justification; with only three data points the transformation choice is arbitrary and inflates R².
The claim that 'the smallest neuron (#6) exhibited the fewest enriched cellular component terms' confounds two explanations—smaller size and poorer retrieval—which the design cannot separate.
No attempt is made to match or covary for neuron location (depth in slice), slice preparation time, or cell-type identity.

questions: Can you provide data from additional neurons in the gigaseal-preserved category to support the correlation between capacitance and protein identifications? How many more recordings would be needed for a minimally convincing regression?

How many neurons were patched in total, and what proportion were excluded from analysis (e.g., because the soma could not be retrieved or the sample was lost)? Is there any systematic bias in which neurons succeeded or failed retrieval?
The PCA in Figure 6A shows clustering; have you tested whether the clusters correspond to measured confounds such as neuron depth, time after slice preparation, or cell size (from DIC images)?

For the SynGO enrichment comparisons: were the gene lists used for each neuron normalised for the number of detected proteins? Could the apparent lack of synaptic enrichment in neuron #6 simply reflect lower total protein IDs rather than a selective loss?

weaknesses.text: Claim that Refs [8] and [9] adopted an "all-or-nothing" inclusion strategy cannot be verified from the cited abstracts alone; the full method sections were not accessible.

Claim that mPFC L2/3 pyramidal neurons were chosen for "its relatively large soma, its rich synaptic proteome" is attributed to Refs [10] and [11], which do not document soma size or synaptic proteome richness.
A very recent competing preprint (Johnson et al. 2026, bioRxiv, doi:10.64898/2026.04.22.720006) describes 'aspiration patch proteomics' and should be discussed if it predates submission.

questions: Can the authors confirm that Refs [8] and [9] explicitly impose the protein-identification thresholds described, and if so, cite the relevant methods sentence?
Was the Johnson et al. 2026 preprint (doi:10.64898/2026.04.22.720006) available at the time this manuscript was prepared, and if not, do the authors consider it relevant to cite in revision?

weaknesses.text: The central quantitative claim — protein identifications correlate with log-transformed capacitance (Figure 3D, F = 1577, R² = 0.998, n = 3) — cannot be independently recomputed from the manuscript as written. The supporting tables (S1–S3) are referenced throughout but the Supporting Information DOI is a literal placeholder ("https://pubs.acs.org/doi/xxxxxxxxxxx/"), so the per-neuron capacitance values and protein counts are not accessible. With n = 3, the correlation is also statistically fragile (data_analysis's call), but from a reproducibility standpoint the raw values must be in the deposit for the claim to be checkable. The MassIVE/PXD accession is given, but I cannot verify it resolves; the placeholder DOI is verifiably broken.

The SynGO enrichment analysis (Figures 4B–C, 6B; Tables S2–S3) is not reproducible as specified. The manuscript states "Gene set enrichment analyses were performed on gene lists derived from DIA-NN's protein-level output" but does not give the SynGO database version, the enrichment algorithm, the background distribution, or the minimum gene-set size. The custom scripts are said to be "available at https://github.com/LarryThePharmacologist" — a user profile URL with no repository name, commit hash, or tag. An independent group cannot know which code version produced the reported enrichment terms.

The PCA (Figure 6A) that supports the claim that retrieval outcomes cluster by proteomic content is underspecified. The manuscript does not state the preprocessing applied to the protein intensity matrix (normalization, imputation, scaling) before PCA, nor which script produces the figure. Without this, the clustering pattern cannot be reproduced.
R package versions (ComplexHeatmap, ggplot2, UpSetR) are not specified — SOFT.
UniProt reference proteome is given only as "downloaded 2024" with no release number — SOFT.
No figure-to-script mapping is provided for any key figure; the manuscript never names a script that produces a specific figure — HARD.
The "performed as previously described [10, 26-31]" citations resolve to published procedures, which is acceptable, but I could not verify the references contain the full protocol — SOFT.
The Zenodo DOI for videos is given, but I cannot verify it resolves — SOFT (peripheral artifact).

questions: Can the authors provide a specific repository URL with a commit hash or tag for the custom scripts?
Can the authors provide the resolved DOI for the Supporting Information, and confirm Tables S1–S3 are accessible there?
Can the authors specify the SynGO database version and the exact GSEA parameters (algorithm, background, minimum gene-set size) used for the enrichment analysis?

weaknesses.text: The central novelty claim — that monitoring gigaseal preservation during retrieval provides information not available from in situ recordings — rests on n = 3 neurons (Figures 3–4). The correlation between log-transformed capacitance and protein identifications (Figure 3D) is reported with F = 1577, p < 0.05, adjusted R² = 0.998, which is a nearly perfect fit for three points. With three data points, any bivariate linear fit is necessarily high or perfect regardless of biological reality. The authors acknowledge the sample size is small, but the interpretive framework derived from these data (e.g., that spike integrity maps to synaptic enrichment) is presented as a general principle. At present, it is an observation on three cells. The claim that gigaseal preservation is a *practical indicator* (as stated in the Conclusions) — rather than a plausible but untested hypothesis — requires replication in a larger, independent cohort.

The claimed differentiation from prior patch-SCP work is less sharp than it appears. The Choi, Polter & Nemes (2022) *Analytical Chemistry* paper already demonstrated patch-clamp proteomics from single neurons in acute brain slices, including detection of membrane and synaptic proteins. The Lee et al. (2024) *Acta Physiologica* paper applied it to locus coeruleus with sex comparisons. Both used cytoplasmic aspiration rather than whole-soma retrieval, which is a real methodological difference. But the authors do not explicitly state what new *biological or technical insight* whole-soma retrieval enables that cytoplasmic aspiration could not, other than higher protein counts. The Ghatak et al. (2024) *Advanced Science* paper used whole-soma retrieval from iPSC neurons, which is a different system, but already demonstrated the principle of somal collection for proteomics. The manuscript would benefit from a head-to-head comparison — even if qualitative — of what the present framework adds versus what was already achievable with cytoplasmic aspiration in slices.

The “shotgun” indiscriminate-collection strategy is presented as novel, but its value depends on whether it produces interpretable data for the majority of collected cells. As shown in Figure 6, neurons #11 and #12 (torn) clustered separately and had low utility, and several other neurons (e.g., #6, #10) lacked synaptic enrichment despite high protein counts. The authors use this to argue that comprehensive analysis reveals compromised retrievals, but this is circular: a “shotgun” strategy that includes all outcomes can only reveal which outcomes are compromised if one already has a standard for what “good” looks like — and that standard is defined by the gigaseal-preserved neurons (n = 3). Without an independent validation set, the classification of “high-context” vs. “low-context” retrievals risks being post-hoc rationalization.
The manuscript repeatedly uses “tended to be associated with” language for correlations drawn from n = 3, which is statistically and rhetorically too strong for the evidence.

The claim that “retrieval mechanics, rather than in situ electrophysiology alone, limit whether proteins associated with excitability and synaptic function are recovered” is stated as a conclusion but is largely a restatement of the study design — it is not surprising that mechanical retrieval loss degrades recovery; what is missing is a quantitative threshold or guideline for when a retrieval is “good enough” for a given biological question.

The ion channel, GPCR and transporter detection lists (Figures 7, S4, S5) are presented as a demonstration of capability, but the sparse and variable recovery (4–27 ion channel subunits per cell) is not benchmarked against the expected expression of these proteins in mPFC L2/3 pyramidal neurons, so a reader cannot assess whether the coverage is good or poor.

The framework in Figure 1 is descriptive and useful, but novelty of a *framework* is limited — frameworks become contributions when they enable predictions or decisions that were not possible before, and the manuscript does not demonstrate such a use case (e.g., a prospective rule for excluding low-quality retrievals).

A concurrent preprint from Johnson et al. (2026, “Proteome-Driven Phenotyping of Identified Single Neurons in Intact Brain Tissue by Aspiration Patch Proteomics”) appears to address a closely related question (patch-proteomics in intact tissue) and is not discussed or compared. While it posted later, its existence underscores the fast-moving nature of the field and the need to clearly stake out what the present work uniquely contributes.

The claim that “patch-SCP can be used to assess soma retrieval” (from the Abstract) is a modest operational claim and uncontroversial; it does not require novelty scrutiny. The larger framing claims are where the weaknesses above apply.

questions: Can the authors provide the raw data points and correlation statistics (e.g., bootstrapped confidence intervals) for the capacitance–protein-identifications relationship in Figure 3D, given that R² = 0.998 with three points is a mathematical necessity for any tight scatter and is not meaningful?

What is the minimal detectable fold-change or expression level threshold for the transmembrane proteins reported in Figure 7, and how does this compare to the expected copy number of GABRA1, SCN2A, GRM3 etc. in a single mPFC L2/3 pyramidal soma?

Would the authors be willing to prospectively define an inclusion criterion for “high-context retrieval” based on the current data (e.g., capacitance > X pF, spiking amplitude > Y mV during relocation) and test it on an independent set of neurons?

weaknesses.text: The capacitance–protein-count correlation (n = 3) is confounded by retrieval damage, and the reported precision is misleading. The three neurons differ in retrieval integrity: neuron #6 was partially aspirated, neuron #7 had compromised spiking, neuron #4 was the ideal retrieval. The capacitance used in the correlation is the during-retrieval value (Figure 3C), measured after the aspiration for neuron #6. Partial aspiration reduces both the measured capacitance (membrane lost) and the protein count, so the reported correlation (F = 1577, adjusted R² = 0.998, n = 3) is equally consistent with 'retrieval damage reduces both capacitance and protein recovery' as with 'soma size predicts recovery.' The authors interpret it as the latter, but the design cannot distinguish them. With n = 3, the line is defined by three points and adjusted R² = 0.998 is misleadingly precise. What would settle it: report the change in capacitance from in situ to during-retrieval for each neuron (a direct measure of damage) alongside the correlation, or restrict the correlation to neurons with comparable retrieval integrity.

The 'decoupling' claim rests on a null result in an unpowered sample. 'Neither log-transformed capacitance nor RM correlated with protein identifications (p > 0.05; n = 6)' is presented as evidence that retrieval loss decouples proteomic measurements from electrophysiology. With n = 6, the power to detect a correlation is minimal; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Moreover, the n = 6 pools heterogeneous outcomes (no gigaseal, gigaseal lost, torn), and the torn neurons' low protein counts could dilute any genuine size effect. The manuscript itself concedes larger samples are needed, yet the conclusion is stated as established. Reframe this as preliminary, or add an equivalence test if the claim is that the correlation is truly absent.

The spike-integrity/synaptic-protein association is descriptive, not tested. The claim that 'preservation of active properties during retrieval is associated with recovery of synaptic proteins' rests on a qualitative comparison of SynGO enrichment across three neurons (Figure 4). No statistical test compares enrichment across neurons; the pattern (neuron #4 richest, neuron #6 lacking synaptic signaling) is anecdotal at n = 3. There is also a partial circularity: spike integrity is itself a marker of retrieval quality, so both spike integrity and synaptic protein recovery are consequences of the same retrieval damage — the association is partly built into the design.
The '25–50% of the soma could be lost' estimate has no stated derivation; specify how it was computed from the capacitance changes in Figure 3C.
SynGO enrichment reports Q-values < 0.05, implying FDR correction, but the correction method is never named; state it.
PCA (Figure 6A) gives no scaling, number of components, or variance explained; the clustering interpretation is qualitative.
Exact p-values are not reported (e.g., 'p < 0.05' for F = 1577 with df = 1,1); report exact values.
The log transformation of capacitance is not justified; with n = 3, the transformation choice can materially affect the fit.
No power analysis or equivalence testing accompanies the 'no correlation' claims; acceptable for a proof-of-concept only if explicitly framed as preliminary.

questions: For the capacitance–protein correlation, can you report the capacitance change from in situ to during-retrieval for each of the three neurons? This would directly test whether retrieval damage, rather than soma size, drives the correlation.
What is the derivation of the 25–50% soma loss estimate from Figure 3C?
Which multiple-comparison correction was applied to the SynGO Q-values?

weaknesses.text: The claim that capacitance correlates with protein identifications (Figure 3D) is stated as a general finding ('soma size... plays a more direct role in protein recovery') but rests on n=3 neurons; the reported F=1577, adjusted R²=0.998 is a regression on three points, and the text does not state that this cannot distinguish a real relationship from noise. The authors should report the raw data points and explicitly scale the claim to n=3.

The inference that spike integrity during retrieval is 'associated with the recovery of synaptic proteins' (Figure 4) is presented as a general association but rests on one neuron per condition (neuron #4 stable, #7 reduced amplitude, #6 single spike). The sentence 'preservation of active properties during retrieval is associated with recovery of synaptic proteins' should be explicitly framed as a hypothesis-generating observation, not a demonstrated association.

The PCA clustering (Figure 6A) is used to support the claim that torn neurons cluster apart and that neuron #6 groups with no-gigaseal neurons, but the text does not report the variance explained by the first two principal components or whether clustering reflects retrieval quality rather than total protein yield driving the first component. A reader cannot determine what the axes represent or how much of the variance the separation captures.

Several quantitative claims state direction without the actual quantity: e.g., 'torn or aspirated neurons produced the fewest detected proteins' and '1,400-2,300 proteins detected per soma' for no-gigaseal retrievals are given, but the torn-neuron protein counts are not stated, so the reader cannot compare the categories quantitatively.

The estimate that '25-50% of the soma could be lost over the course of collection' is presented without any description of how this was measured or derived, leaving the reader unable to determine what evidence supports the range.

The term 'shotgun patch-SCP' is introduced in the abstract and used throughout but is never formally defined at first use; the reader must infer it means indiscriminate collection of all patch attempts, which is stated only later in the Results.

questions: Could the authors report the raw capacitance and protein identification values for the three gigaseal-preserved neurons, so readers can assess the correlation without relying on the regression fit?
For the PCA in Figure 6A, could the authors report the variance explained by the first two principal components and state whether the clustering is robust to normalization or scaling choices?
How was the 25-50% soma loss estimate derived, and what measurement supports it?
